title: The Greenhouse Effect and Climate Feedbacks
subtitle: How a thin layer of gas keeps Earth warm, why adding more of it warms us further, and which loops make the warming grow
intro: Climate change is often explained as a list of facts. It makes far more sense as a **structure**: energy flows in and out, a few gases slow the way out, human activity adds those gases, and some consequences loop back and add even more warming.
First you will see the whole map, one region at a time. Then it comes apart and you put it back together from memory. That second part is where the learning sticks.

clusters.name: How the trap works
clusters.description: The physical chain from sunlight to a warmer surface: energy comes in as sunlight and tries to leave as infrared heat.

clusters.name: Greenhouse gases
clusters.description: The gases that let sunlight through but absorb outgoing infrared, and the effect they produce together.

clusters.name: Human sources
clusters.description: The human activities that add greenhouse gases to the air faster than nature removes them.

clusters.name: Carbon sinks
clusters.description: Natural stores that take carbon dioxide out of the air, slowing its build-up.

clusters.name: Feedback loops
clusters.description: Changes that warming itself sets off, which then add to (or, rarely, subtract from) the warming.

clusters.name: Consequences
clusters.description: What a warmer world, and a more acidic ocean, mean on the ground.

nodes.label: Greenhouse effect
nodes.definition: Gases in the air let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat, keeping Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would otherwise be.
nodes.note: The natural greenhouse effect is why Earth is habitable at all: without it the average surface temperature would be about −18 °C. The problem is the **enhanced** effect: every extra molecule of CO₂ or methane slows the escape of heat a little more.
nodes.example: A car parked in the sun: light gets in through the glass, the heat it turns into struggles to get out.

nodes.label: Incoming sunlight
nodes.definition: Short-wave energy from the Sun; on average about 340 watts reach each square metre at the top of the atmosphere.
nodes.note: Greenhouse gases are almost transparent to this short-wave light, so most of it passes straight through the air.

nodes.label: Warm surface
nodes.definition: Land and ocean absorb the sunlight that is not reflected, and warm up.
nodes.note: About half of incoming sunlight is absorbed at the surface; the rest is reflected or absorbed in the atmosphere.

nodes.label: Infrared radiation
nodes.definition: The heat a warm surface gives off, as long-wave radiation we cannot see.
nodes.note: Every warm object glows in infrared. The warmer it is, the more it emits. This is the energy greenhouse gases intercept.

nodes.label: Back-radiation
nodes.definition: Infrared that greenhouse gases re-emit downward, warming the surface a second time.
nodes.note: A gas molecule that absorbs infrared re-emits it in a random direction, so roughly half heads back down.

nodes.label: Escape to space
nodes.definition: The infrared that makes it out; for a stable climate, outgoing energy must match incoming energy.
nodes.note: When less escapes than arrives, the planet gains energy and warms until it radiates enough to balance again.

nodes.label: Albedo
nodes.definition: The share of sunlight a surface reflects straight back to space. Bright ice reflects a lot; dark ocean very little.
nodes.example: Fresh snow reflects about 80–90% of sunlight; open ocean only about 6%.

nodes.label: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
nodes.definition: A long-lived greenhouse gas and the main driver of human-caused warming.
nodes.note: CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million before industry to over 420 today. A large share of what we emit stays in the air for centuries.

nodes.label: Methane (CH₄)
nodes.definition: A shorter-lived greenhouse gas that traps about 80 times more heat than CO₂ over its first 20 years.
nodes.note: Methane breaks down in about a decade, so cutting it slows warming quickly.

nodes.label: Water vapour
nodes.definition: The most abundant greenhouse gas; how much the air holds is set by temperature.
nodes.note: We do not add water vapour directly in any meaningful amount. Warmer air simply holds more of it: about 7% more per degree.

nodes.label: Burning fossil fuels
nodes.definition: Coal, oil and gas burned for power, heat and transport, releasing carbon stored for millions of years.
nodes.note: The largest single source of human CO₂ emissions, roughly three-quarters of the total.

nodes.label: Deforestation
nodes.definition: Clearing forests, usually for farmland, which releases their carbon and removes a sink.
nodes.note: It hurts twice: the trees' carbon goes into the air, and the forest stops absorbing more.

nodes.label: Farming & livestock
nodes.definition: Cattle digestion, rice paddies and manure release methane; fertiliser releases nitrous oxide.
nodes.example: A single cow belches roughly 100 kg of methane a year.

nodes.label: Ocean uptake
nodes.definition: Seawater dissolves CO₂ from the air; the ocean has absorbed about a quarter of human emissions.
nodes.note: This slows warming, but the dissolved CO₂ turns into carbonic acid.

nodes.label: Forests & soils
nodes.definition: Plants take in CO₂ to grow, and store carbon in wood, roots and soil.
nodes.note: Land ecosystems absorb roughly another quarter of human emissions, as long as they are left standing.

nodes.label: Ice–albedo feedback
nodes.definition: Melting ice exposes darker water and land, which absorb more sunlight and cause more melting.
nodes.note: One of the main reasons the Arctic is warming about three to four times faster than the global average.

nodes.label: Water-vapour feedback
nodes.definition: Warming puts more water vapour in the air, which traps more heat, which warms further.
nodes.note: Roughly doubles the warming that CO₂ alone would cause; it is the strongest feedback we know of.

nodes.label: Permafrost thaw
nodes.definition: Frozen Arctic ground thaws, and microbes break down ancient plant matter into methane and CO₂.
nodes.note: Permafrost holds about twice as much carbon as the atmosphere does today.

nodes.label: Cloud feedback
nodes.definition: Warming changes how many clouds form and where; low clouds cool, high thin clouds warm.
nodes.note: The most uncertain feedback, though the best current estimate is that it adds a little warming overall.

nodes.label: Global warming
nodes.definition: The rise in Earth's average surface temperature, about 1.2 °C since the late 1800s.
nodes.note: A global average hides much larger changes in some places and seasons.

nodes.label: Melting ice
nodes.definition: Shrinking sea ice, glaciers and ice sheets as temperatures rise.
nodes.example: Arctic summer sea ice has lost roughly 40% of its area since 1979.

nodes.label: Sea-level rise
nodes.definition: Oceans rise as land ice melts into them and as warmer water expands.
nodes.note: Global sea level has risen about 20 cm since 1900, and the rate is speeding up.

nodes.label: Ocean acidification
nodes.definition: Dissolved CO₂ makes seawater more acidic, harming shell-building life such as corals and plankton.
nodes.note: It is a chemistry problem, not a heat problem: it would happen even if CO₂ caused no warming at all.

nodes.label: Heatwaves & extremes
nodes.definition: More frequent and intense heatwaves, heavy downpours and droughts.
nodes.example: A heatwave that used to happen once in 50 years now happens about every 10.

edges.explanation: Sunlight passes through the mostly transparent air and is absorbed by land and ocean, which warm up.
About 30% of incoming sunlight is reflected straight back to space by clouds, ice and bright surfaces, and never heats anything.
Any warm object radiates heat. Earth's surface sheds its energy as long-wave infrared.
Some infrared slips out through gaps in the gases' absorption; the rest is caught on the way.
Infrared absorbed by greenhouse gases is re-emitted in all directions, and about half comes back down.
The surface is warmed twice, by sunlight and by returned heat. That second helping is the greenhouse effect at work.
CO₂ molecules vibrate at exactly the frequencies of part of Earth's infrared glow, so they soak it up.
More CO₂ means more infrared caught on its way out, so the greenhouse effect grows stronger.
Methane absorbs infrared too, and molecule for molecule it is far more potent than CO₂.
Water vapour accounts for roughly half of the natural greenhouse effect, more than any other gas.
The greenhouse effect is not a lid; it works by gases sending part of the outgoing heat back down.
Strengthen the effect and less heat escapes than arrives, so the planet warms until balance returns at a higher temperature.
Burning coal, oil and gas returns carbon that was locked underground for millions of years, all within a few centuries.
Burning or rotting cleared trees puts their stored carbon into the air as CO₂.
Every cleared hectare is a hectare that no longer absorbs CO₂.
Microbes in cattle stomachs, flooded rice fields and manure heaps produce methane.
The ocean dissolves about a quarter of the CO₂ we emit, which slows its build-up in the air.
Growing plants pull CO₂ out of the air through photosynthesis and store the carbon.
CO₂ dissolved in seawater forms carbonic acid. The sink that slows warming is also the source of acidification.
Both come from CO₂, but acidification is chemistry, not heat: it would happen even if CO₂ trapped no warmth at all.
Warmer air and water melt sea ice, glaciers and the edges of the great ice sheets.
Each patch of ice that melts uncovers darker sea or rock underneath, starting the ice–albedo loop.
Dark water and rock reflect far less sunlight than bright ice, so Earth's overall albedo goes down.
Less reflection means more sunlight absorbed, which means more warming and more melting: a self-reinforcing loop.
Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour per degree, which sets the water-vapour feedback going.
The feedback is simply more water vapour in the air, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas.
As the Arctic warms, ground that has been frozen for thousands of years starts to thaw each summer.
Thawed soil lets microbes digest ancient plant matter, and in waterlogged ground they make methane.
Where thawed soil is drier, microbes break the old carbon down into CO₂ instead.
A warmer, wetter atmosphere changes how many clouds form, how high, and where.
Low clouds reflect sunlight and cool; high thin clouds trap heat and warm. The net effect is probably a small extra warming.
Melting land ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctica) adds water to the ocean. Melting sea ice does not, because it already floats.
Water takes up more room as it warms; this thermal expansion is about a third of sea-level rise so far.
A small shift in the average makes the hot extremes much more frequent, and warmer air carries more water into downpours.

tour.title: The big idea
tour.text: At the centre is the **greenhouse effect**: certain gases slow the escape of heat. Turn it up, and the planet warms. Everything else on this map either explains that link, feeds it, or follows from it.

tour.title: How the trap works
tour.text: Sunlight heats the surface. The warm surface glows in **infrared**. Some escapes to space; the rest is caught by gases and sent back down as back-radiation, warming the surface a second time.

tour.title: The gases that do it
tour.text: CO₂, methane and water vapour all absorb infrared. Water vapour does the most work, but CO₂ is the one we are turning up, and it lasts for centuries.

tour.title: Where the extra comes from
tour.text: Burning fossil fuels, clearing forests and farming add gases faster than the ocean and the land can take them back out. The sinks soak up about half of our CO₂; the other half piles up.

tour.title: Loops that amplify
tour.text: Warming sets off changes that cause **more** warming: melting ice darkens the surface, warmer air holds more water vapour, thawing permafrost releases methane. Clouds are the wild card.

tour.title: What it means for us
tour.text: A warmer world brings rising seas and fiercer extremes. And the ocean pays twice: the CO₂ it absorbs turns its water more acidic, a harm that **contrasts with** warming because it is chemistry, not heat.

rebuild.intro: Three concepts have floated free of their clusters, a few labels have gone blank, one link has vanished and one now says something false. Put the map back together from memory.

tasks.hint: Ask what each one **does**: is it a gas that traps heat, something that soaks up carbon, or a change that warming sets off?
tasks.why: Clusters group concepts by role. Methane is a greenhouse gas; forests and soils store carbon, so they are a sink; thawing permafrost is a feedback, because warming starts it and it then adds more warming.

tasks.prompt: Put the steps of the heat trap in order, from the Sun to the second warming.
tasks.hint: Start with what arrives from the Sun, and end with what comes back down.
tasks.why: Sunlight is short-wave and passes through the air; the ground absorbs it and re-emits long-wave infrared; gases catch some of that and send it back down. More gas means more comes back, so the surface warms.

tasks.hint: Think about what a growing tree is made of, and where that carbon came from.
tasks.why: Plants build themselves out of carbon taken from CO₂ in the air. That is what makes forests and soils a sink.

options.label: emit
options.why: Forests only release CO₂ when they burn, rot or are cleared; that link belongs to deforestation. A standing, growing forest takes CO₂ in.

options.label: strengthen
options.why: That is what greenhouse gases do to the greenhouse effect. Forests weaken it, by taking CO₂ out of the air.

options.label: contrasts with
options.why: They are directly linked, not merely compared: forests change how much CO₂ is in the air.

tasks.hint: Frozen Arctic ground holds old plant matter. Which gas do microbes make from it when the ground thaws and stays waterlogged?
tasks.why: Thawing permafrost lets microbes break down ancient organic matter, releasing methane (and CO₂). That is why it is a feedback: warming causes the thaw, and the thaw causes more warming.

tasks.hint: Is open ocean darker or lighter than ice?
tasks.why: Ice is bright and reflects most sunlight; open water and bare ground are dark. As ice melts, Earth's albedo goes **down**, so more sunlight is absorbed. That is exactly what makes this loop amplify warming.

tasks.hint: It sits with the carbon sinks, and it is also the cause of acidification.
tasks.why: The ocean dissolves about a quarter of the CO₂ we emit. That slows warming, but the dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which is why the same concept links to both the sinks and acidification.

options.label: Sea-level rise
options.why: Sea-level rise is a consequence of melting land ice and warming water; it does not take any CO₂ out of the air.

options.label: Water vapour
options.why: Water vapour is a gas in the air, not the sea taking up carbon, and it adds to the greenhouse effect rather than removing CO₂.

options.label: Cloud feedback
options.why: Clouds change how much sunlight is reflected; they do not remove CO₂, and they sit with the feedbacks, not the sinks.

tasks.hint: There are two kinds of clouds with opposite effects. What does that make the overall effect?
tasks.why: Low, thick clouds reflect sunlight and cool; high, thin clouds trap heat and warm. Because both change as the climate warms, scientists can only say the net effect is probably a small amplification.

options.label: always cools
options.why: Low clouds do cool, but high thin clouds warm; the net effect is uncertain and probably slightly warming.

options.label: has no effect on
options.why: Clouds have large effects in both directions; the uncertainty is about which wins, not whether they matter.

tasks.hint: Both start with CO₂. Is acidification caused by heat?
tasks.why: Ocean acidification and global warming share a cause (CO₂) but work in completely different ways: one is chemistry in the water, the other is trapped heat. That is a contrast, not a cause.

options.label: is caused by
options.why: Warming does not make water acidic; dissolved CO₂ does. Acidification would happen even if CO₂ trapped no heat.

options.label: causes
options.why: A more acidic ocean harms marine life, but it does not heat the planet.

reflection.prompt: If you could keep only three links from this map, which would they be?

keyEdges.why: This is the human lever. Most of the extra greenhouse effect since the 1800s traces back to this single link, and it is the one we can switch off.
This turns emissions into trapped heat. Because CO₂ lasts for centuries, what we emit accumulates: the climate responds to the total, not the yearly amount.
Feedbacks are why a modest push becomes a large change. Take this kind of link away and warming would be roughly half as big.

reflection.closing: Cause, mechanism, amplifier: with those three links in mind you can rebuild most of the rest of the map yourself.

glossary.meaning: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. 0 is perfectly dark, 1 is a perfect mirror.
Long-wave radiation that warm objects give off; invisible to us, but felt as heat.
A gas that lets sunlight through but absorbs outgoing infrared: mainly water vapour, CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide.
A change that a process causes and that then acts back on the process. **Amplifying** feedbacks make it bigger; damping ones make it smaller.
Anything that takes up more carbon than it releases, such as the ocean, forests and soils.
Ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years in a row, often for thousands.
Infrared emitted downward by the atmosphere towards the surface.
Parts per million: 420 ppm of CO₂ means 420 of every million air molecules are CO₂.

summary.heading: The map, rebuilt
paragraphs: Sunlight comes in, infrared heat tries to leave, and greenhouse gases send part of it back. Humans have been adding those gases faster than the sinks can remove them, so the planet warms until it can shed as much energy as it receives.
Warming then feeds itself through melting ice, extra water vapour and thawing permafrost. Seeing it as a map makes the key point plain: there is one main lever, and it is upstream of everything else.
